abstract: Quantum simulation promises to advance materials discovery by accurately simulating complex states of matter, their microscopic excitations, and macroscopic response functions. The central challenge in resolving the underlying interacting dynamics is to combine high-fidelity evolution with the sophisticated control necessary to manipulate individual quasi-particles in quantum many-body states. Here, we report on high-precision simulation of both linear and non-linear response functions in a 2D XY spin-1/2 magnet using an analog-digital superconducting processor of up to 97 qubits. By interleaving digital gates with analog evolution precisely characterized via Hamiltonian learning, we selectively excite magnons at tunable energy densities. Measuring first the linear magnon response -- a central probe in neutron-scattering experiments -- we extract temperature-dependent spectra and lifetimes. Our results reveal stark variations in magnon decay rates across the Brillouin zone, with enhancement near van Hove singularities and suppression for edge-localized modes. Next, we perform a suite of nonlinear measurements, including the study of self-scattering mechanisms, as well as pump-probe spectroscopy to directly characterize the magnon interactions. While matrix-product state simulations capture the dynamics well in either small systems or at low temperatures, their predictions become inaccurate away from these limits. This work demonstrates precise simulation of the interacting dynamics in quantum magnets, and provides key insights into quasi-particles and their microscopic scattering mechanisms.
summary: The research reports on achieving high-precision quantum simulation of interacting magnon dynamics in a 2D XY magnet using superconducting qubits. By combining analog evolution with digital gate control, the authors measure key response functions to map out temperature-dependent spectra and scattering mechanisms. This work validates the use of hybrid quantum hardware for probing complex many-body physics relevant to materials science.
main_problem: The central challenge is combining high-fidelity quantum evolution with sophisticated control to accurately simulate complex, interacting dynamics in many-body quantum systems for materials discovery.
main_result: The work demonstrates high-precision simulation of interacting magnon dynamics, revealing strong mode dependence of decay rates and enabling the study of scattering mechanisms inaccessible in simpler regimes.
method: The authors employ an interleaved analog-digital protocol on a superconducting processor to measure time-dependent correlation functions ($\chi_\mu(t)$), comparing these measurements against advanced numerical techniques like Matrix Product States (MPS) and BP-PEPS simulations.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a 2D XY spin-1/2 magnet, realized on an analog-digital superconducting processor of up to 97 qubits. The physics involves quantized spin waves called magnons.
key_observables: Magnon spectra, temperature-dependent decay rates ($\Gamma$), linear and nonlinear response functions ($\chi_\mu(t)$), and mode dependence of scattering mechanisms (e.g., near van Hove singularities).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), energy density ($\epsilon$), qubit count (up to 97 qubits), and simulation fidelity metrics.
main_assumptions: MPS predictions become inaccurate away from low temperatures or small systems; the analysis relies on comparing experimental measurements to approximate numerical simulations like MPS/BP-PEPS.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate Hamiltonian learning circuits, measured time-dependent correlation functions ($\chi_\mu(t)$) matching theory, magnon dispersions showing mode dependence, and power-law fits for temperature dependence of decay rates.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for high-fidelity simulation to detailing the interleaved analog-digital measurement protocol. It then presents results on linear response (spectra/lifetimes), followed by nonlinear measurements (self-scattering), and finally discusses computational limitations using tensor network methods (BP-PEPS) regarding scaling complexity.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges superconducting quantum hardware capabilities with fundamental condensed matter physics problems, providing a blueprint for simulating complex many-body dynamics beyond the reach of current theoretical numerical methods alone.
